en: O friend in the practice of the jewel of the Dharma, by feeling remorse, may you possess prosperity, freedom from illness, and long life;
through the power of the Three Jewels, may there be an increase in the Teaching. (1)
I beg you, sir, to clarify this point regarding my body, which consists of flesh and bone, and has been rendered weak by old age. (2)
"Feed me meat again and again, and give me blood to drink again and again;
let not this emaciation come upon me, for the Yakṣiṇī Old Age clings to me. (3)
I have no strength in my senses; where has my mindfulness gone? My body now trembles like a plantain tree struck by the wind. (4)
(1) Trembling again and again, with his back and neck bent low,
this old man, staff in hand, should always walk with constant faltering.
An unbearable torment revolves through his hands and feet;
drops of sweat flow forth like bubbles upon the water.
Just as the moonlight and the power of vision gradually perish during the dark fortnight, so too [perish] even by means of the eye;
there is no purpose whatsoever [in such a state].
He gasps like a bellows and spits out [his breath] moment by moment;
like a fish cast onto the water, his hand trembles violently. (8)
Alas! The splendor of youth will never return to me;
now, on the stage of the mouth, speech no longer dances as it pleases.
(2) Intelligence has departed, power has vanished, and life passes away day by day;
indeed, Death stands before me with its mouth wide open. 10.
The pen, having rested upon the writing board in the scriptorium, was abandoned along with the thought of composing poetry, like a line drawn upon water. (11)
The books read with such tireless effort now lie dormant in the library;
today, even worms and mice gnaw upon them.
In saṃsāra, everything ends in destruction; even the self does not persist throughout the three states of existence.
Indeed, the absolute liberation taught by the Sage is never subject to decay.
(3) Remembrance of my youth causes intense remorse; alas, I am consumed with grief like an old ox whose tail has been broken. 14.
Having reached seventy-eight years from birth, one is struck down by old age;
beyond this point, how could one compose verse bound in meter and imbued with aesthetic flavor? (15) (4)
